clinicalPearls: An autoimmune deposition dermopathy, most often a manifestation of Graves disease, characterised by firm, non-pitting infiltration of the skin, classically over the pretibial regions and dorsa of the feet.
Almost always occurs with markedly elevated TSH-receptor antibodies and is typically accompanied by Graves ophthalmopathy; it usually appears after the eye disease.
Despite the name, it is a localised mucinosis and is unrelated to the generalised myxoedema of hypothyroidism; most patients are or have been thyrotoxic.
Presents as waxy, skin-coloured to yellow-brown or violaceous plaques and nodules with a peau d'orange texture and prominent hair follicles; a diffuse non-pitting oedematous form also occurs.
Part of the triad with Graves ophthalmopathy and thyroid acropachy (clubbing and periosteal reaction); acropachy signals more severe extrathyroidal disease.
The Koebner phenomenon is relevant, with lesions favouring areas of trauma or dependency; the elephantiasic variant can be disfiguring and disabling.
Diagnosis is usually clinical in a patient with known Graves disease; biopsy shows abundant dermal mucin (glycosaminoglycans) separating collagen bundles.
Management centres on potent topical corticosteroids under occlusion and compression; smoking cessation and control of thyroid disease are important, though the dermopathy runs an independent course.
reference.pathophysiology: Pretibial myxoedema is an extrathyroidal manifestation of autoimmune thyroid disease driven by TSH-receptor autoantibodies. Fibroblasts in the dermis, particularly in the pretibial skin, express the TSH receptor, and stimulation by these autoantibodies, together with insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor signalling and cytokines released by infiltrating activated T lymphocytes, drives fibroblast proliferation and greatly increased synthesis of glycosaminoglycans, chiefly hyaluronic acid. These hydrophilic mucins accumulate in the reticular dermis, drawing in water, separating and fragmenting collagen bundles and producing the firm, non-pitting induration and characteristic plaques. Mechanical factors amplify the process: the dependent position of the lower legs, elevated hydrostatic pressure and local trauma (a Koebner effect) favour mucin deposition and lymphatic compromise in the pretibial region, explaining the anatomical predilection and the severe elephantiasic form. The shared autoimmune target accounts for its close association with Graves ophthalmopathy, where analogous fibroblast activation occurs in orbital tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic venous stasis dermatitis and stasis-related lipodermatosclerosis
Hypertrophic lichen planus and lichen simplex chronicus
Cutaneous mucinoses such as lichen myxoedematosus and scleromyxoedema
Pretibial cellulitis or chronic bacterial infection
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests with TSH-receptor antibody measurement
Skin biopsy demonstrating dermal mucin deposition with special stains for glycosaminoglycans
Assessment and imaging for associated Graves ophthalmopathy
Radiography of the hands to detect thyroid acropachy where suspected
Doppler studies to exclude venous insufficiency or lymphatic obstruction as alternative causes of lower-limb swelling
Antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies to support autoimmune thyroid disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive elephantiasic swelling causing functional impairment or entrapment neuropathy
Ulceration or signs of secondary infection in indurated pretibial skin
Severe coexisting ophthalmopathy threatening vision requiring urgent specialist care
Diagnostic uncertainty where malignancy or an alternative infiltrative process cannot be excluded without biopsy
reference.prognosis: Most cases are mild and either remain stable or improve gradually, sometimes remitting spontaneously over years, and respond partially to topical corticosteroids and compression. The elephantiasic and acropachy-associated forms are more refractory and can be persistently disfiguring and disabling.
pitfalls: Confusing the name with generalised hypothyroid myxoedema and overlooking the underlying Graves disease
Expecting restoration of a euthyroid state to resolve the skin disease, which follows an independent course
Misdiagnosing indurated plaques as cellulitis and prescribing repeated antibiotics
Failing to counsel on smoking cessation, which worsens associated thyroid eye disease
Neglecting compression and Koebner-avoidance advice that influence lower-limb outcomes
references: Endocrinology and thyroid disease clinical guidelines
